title: Checkpoint: Booms and Busts
objective: After this level you can connect inflation, bubbles and recessions, using the 2008 financial crisis as the example.
summary: In 2008, a US housing bubble burst, Lehman Brothers failed and the Great Recession followed, with doubled unemployment and briefly falling prices. Economists still debate why the boom happened.

cards.headline: In 2008, a bubble, a bust and a recession arrived as a package deal.
cards.body: Chapter 7's ideas don't take turns. The 2008 financial crisis put nearly all of them into one story. Time to follow it.

events.label: US home prices more than double, the sharpest rise on record
Home prices start falling; recession begins in December
Consumer prices are lower than a year before

cards.headline: Chapter 7, all in one story
cards.body: Level 68's bubble: risky mortgages, packaged into securities, widened credit and pushed home prices up; then prices fell by over a fifth, bringing defaults and foreclosures. Level 66's cycle: the longest US recession since World War II. Level 67's cyclical unemployment: the jobless rate more than doubled, from under 5% to 10%. Even Level 64's worry appeared, as consumer prices fell over a year for the first time since 1955.

cards.headline: Still argued over
cards.body: Why did the housing boom happen? Economist John Taylor argued that the Fed kept interest rates low for too long. Ben Bernanke answered that this explains only a small part, and pointed to a flood of global savings that pushed interest rates down worldwide. Like the Great Depression, the Great Recession left a clear story of what happened and an open argument about why.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Why economies swing between booms and recessions, and why the causes of big crashes are still argued.
What inflation does to your money, and how a basket of everyday purchases measures it.
Why printing money to pay a government's bills can end in hyperinflation, and why falling prices hurt too.
What GDP counts and leaves out, and how the unemployment rate can miss people who stopped looking.

questions.prompt: Which asset's price boom and bust set off the 2008 crisis?
questions.explanation: US home prices more than doubled from 1998 to 2006, then fell by over a fifth.

questions.prompt: What makes the 2000s housing boom a bubble in Level 68's sense?

options.label: Home prices rose slowly and never fell
options.rationale: Prices fell by over a fifth.

options.label: The government fixed every house price
Prices ran far above fundamentals, then fell
Builders stopped making new homes
options.rationale: The story is about prices and credit.

questions.explanation: Easy credit pushed prices far above what fundamentals justified; then they fell by over a fifth.

questions.prompt: US unemployment rose from under 5% to 10% in the Great Recession. Which type from Level 67 was that rise?

options.label: Frictional
options.rationale: That exists even in good times, as people switch jobs.

options.label: Structural
options.rationale: That's a skills mismatch, not a recession effect.

options.label: Seasonal
options.rationale: Seasons don't explain a recession's job losses.

questions.explanation: Unemployment that rises in a recession and falls in an expansion is cyclical.

questions.prompt: US consumer prices fell over the year to March 2009. By Level 64's logic, why did that worry economists?

options.label: Falling prices can make people put off buying
Falling prices always cause hyperinflation
options.rationale: Hyperinflation is the opposite: prices soaring.

options.label: Cheaper goods mean shops run out of stock
options.rationale: Deflation comes with weak spending, not shortages.

options.label: Lower prices make every loan smaller
options.rationale: Debts stay fixed in dollars and get heavier in real terms.

questions.explanation: When prices fall, people delay purchases, cutting activity, income and growth.

questions.prompt: What do economists still argue about in the 2008 story?

options.label: Whether home prices ever fell
options.rationale: They fell by over a fifth.

options.label: Whether Lehman Brothers really went bankrupt
Whether there was a recession at all
options.rationale: It ran from December 2007 to June 2009.

options.label: How much low interest rates fed the boom

questions.explanation: Taylor blamed the Fed's long spell of low rates; Bernanke said that explains little and pointed to global savings.
